title: Nexus
subtitle: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
author: Yuval Noah Harari
lead: Information connects people more than it informs them. Networks built on it give power faster than wisdom. AI, the first non-human member of these networks, needs institutions that correct their own errors.

chapters.title: Documents: The Bite of the Paper Tigers
Decisions: A Brief History of Democracy and Totalitarianism

screens.label: Core idea
screens.text: Democracy spreads information across many independent nodes and can correct its own errors. Totalitarianism pulls all information to one centre that claims it cannot be wrong. The difference is how information flows, not only who votes.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: A healthy democracy is noisy on purpose: its friction is how it finds its mistakes.

screens.alt: Two networks. In a democracy, government, courts, free press, citizens, experts and parties are linked to each other and to public debate. In a totalitarian state, army, police, press, courts, factories and citizens all report to the party-state.

items.title: Democracy is a conversation
items.text: Not only majority rule. It needs free media, courts and rights, so that errors can be exposed and losers can try again.

items.title: Populism
items.text: Claims that one leader alone speaks for "the people", and attacks the courts, media and experts that check power.

items.title: The totalitarian trinity
items.text: Party, state and secret police watch each other and everyone else, so no independent source of information can grow.

items.title: Scale needs media
items.text: Large democracies became possible only with newspapers, telegraph and radio, the same tools that made totalitarianism possible.

screens.label: The logic
steps: Politics is a question of how information flows.
Democracy spreads information; dictatorship centralises it.
Central networks block bad news on its way up.
Mass media made both mass democracy and totalitarianism possible.
Judge a democracy by its free conversation, not only by elections.

items.title: Stalin's "kulaks"
items.text: A category invented at the centre and imposed on farmers.

items.title: Three Mile Island and Chernobyl
items.text: Open reporting brought fast learning; secrecy, a bigger disaster.

questions.q: Why can a country hold elections and still not be a democracy, in Harari's terms?
questions.a: Democracy is a free conversation protected by rights, courts and media. Without them, elections only confirm the ruler.

questions.q: Why does bad news travel badly in a centralised network?
questions.a: Every message must pass through the centre, and people fear reporting failure, so errors stay hidden until they grow.

questions.q: Which technologies made mass democracy possible, and why did they also help dictators?
questions.a: Newspapers, telegraph and radio let millions share one conversation, and also let a centre watch and control millions.
